articles.title: What Age Can a Child Walk to School Alone
articles.h1: What Age Can A Child Walk To School Alone?
articles.meta: What age can a child walk to school alone? Pediatric guidance says 10, but your child's crossing habits and your actual route decide it. Assess both today.
articles.excerpt: The morning I remember best went like this. Shoes missing, the toddler's daycare bag still on the counter, a meeting at 9:00 that I had already told two people I would be early for, and my oldest standing by the door asking, again, to walk. She had been asking for weeks. She knew the route. She stopped at the corner without being told, every time. And still, standing there with car keys in one hand, the question of what age a child can walk to school alone felt like something I wanted an official answer to rather than a judgment call I had to make in the next ninety seconds. There is an answer, and it starts at 10. Where it goes after that depends on two things you can check yourself: what your child does on the actual route, and what the route does to them. What age can a child walk to school alone according to pediatric guidance The American Academy of Pediatrics put the marker at 10. In its 2009 policy statement on pedestrian safety, the AAP wrote that "on the basis of developmental considerations and currently available research data, the American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that children should not be unsupervised pedestrians before 10 years of age, except in limited situations." Notice the shape of that sentence. The AAP describes a floor with exceptions written into it, rather than a birthday that flips a switch. So when parents ask what age a kid can walk to school alone, 10 is where the assessment opens, not where it closes. A child of 11 on a route with four uncontrolled crossings and a 40 mph road may be less ready than a child of 10 walking three blocks of residential sidewalk. Age tells you when to start looking properly. What you see on the walk tells you the rest.
